e: To 'strike while the iron is hot' means to make use of an opportunity immediately. To 'gain ground' means becoming more popular or accepted. 'Shot in the dark' means a guess. 'Roll up the sleeves' means prepare to fight or work. Option b) gives a meaningfully appropriate sentence which indicates that the mayor gained support from the teacher's union. Hence, b) is the correct answer

t: Which word in the given sentence is the ANTONYM of nibble? "They sprinted across the floor and leaped up to the elevated platforms, poking their soft muzzles into the stanchions to gobble the grain."
o: muzzles
elevated
sprinted
gobble
e: "Nibble" (छोटे-छोटे टुकड़ों में खाना) का antonym है "Gobble" (जल्दी-जल्दी खाना) — eating food too fast। "Muzzles" (थूथन), "Elevated" (ऊँचा), और "Sprinted" (तेज़ दौड़ना) असंबंधित हैं।

t: Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom: "The threat of the pandemic is not just a CRY IN THE WILDERNESS."
o: an unheeded warning
mourning for the loss
tears of sorrow
spreading rumours
e: "A cry in the wilderness" (अनसुनी चेतावनी) — इसका अर्थ है someone who points out dangers in a situation but nobody pays attention। Example: "He was a voice crying in the wilderness as he tried to expose the vast corruption." "Mourning" (शोक), "Tears of sorrow" (दुःख के आँसू), और "Spreading rumours" (अफवाह फैलाना) गलत हैं।

t:
Select the most appropriate idiom to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. 
 The peasants worked the whole day in the fields and stopped working in the evening and went to their homes.
o: gave it a whirl
put ice on it
ran around in circles
called it a day
e: D)and stopped working in the evening and went to their homes'के बदले 'called it a day' का प्रयोग होगा क्योंकि यह idiom 'दिन का काम समाप्त कर देना' के अर्थ में प्रयोग होता है।

t: Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute italicised words in the given sentence The one-hour period after his lunch is his time for a short sleep.
o: on thin ice
once in a blue moon
on cloud nine
forty winks
e: Option (d) is the correct answer. The idiom 'forty winks' means 'a short sleep, especially during the day'. The meanings of the other idioms are- On thin ice means- in a risky situation. Once in a blue moon means - rarely. On cloud nine- extremely happy.

t: Which of the following idioms means 'to initiate something or set a process in motion'?
o: Hold your horses
Get the ball rolling
Jump on the bandwagon
Throw a spanner in the works
e:
a) Hold your horses - To wait; to be patient before doing something.
b) Get the ball rolling - To start something, especially a process or activity that involves other people.
c) Jump on the bandwagon - To join a popular activity or trend.
d) Throw a spanner in the works (UK) / Throw a monkey wrench in the works (US) - To do something that prevents a plan or activity from succeeding.
Hence, option (b) is the answer.

t: Read the sentence carefully and select the most suitable idiom to fill in the blank. The renowned publisher decided to withdraw a book from the market. No one was interested in the book as the arguments presented were ______.
o: high and mighty
out of the woods
beside the mark
under the rose
e: "Beside the mark" (अप्रासंगिक, अशुद्ध) का अर्थ है irrelevant or inaccurate। यहाँ arguments relevant नहीं थे। Correct Sentence: ...arguments presented were beside the mark.

t: Select the most appropriate idiom (in the context) to fill in the sentence. Factory owners are protesting because they think that the government has _________ of plastic manufacturing companies by closing their factories in big cities.
o: Separated the wheat from the chaff
Been barking up the wrong tree
Upset the apple cart
Made no bones
e: "Upset the apple cart" (योजना बिगाड़ना) means to ruin plans or arrangements; to spoil something. Factory owners feel the government has spoiled their plans — perfect fit.

t:
Identify the idiom/phrase that can best substitute the underlined segment. 
 You showed me your true personality when you asked me to get out of the house at midnight.
o: true colours
bed of roses
hot potato
white elephant
e: A) "true Personality" के बदले "true colours" का प्रयोग होगा क्योंकि यह इडियम व्यक्ति की असली पहचान या व्यक्तित्व को दर्शाने के लिए प्रयुक्त होता है जो आमतौर पर छुपा रहता है; जैसे— You showed me your true colours when you acted in that way.

t: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. LIVING IN A FOOL'S PARADISE
o: To be fooled by someone
To live in a world of imagination
To live with a fool
To believe wrongly that your situation is good
e: "Living in a fool's paradise" means to believe wrongly and unrealistically that one's situation is good or satisfactory, when in reality it is not. (Hindi: झूठी खुशी में जीना / भ्रम में रहना) Example: She looks much happier but surely she is living in a fool's paradise. Historical note: The phrase first appeared in the 'Paston Letters' (1462) and was later used by Shakespeare in 'Romeo and Juliet' (1592). Common confusion: "world of imagination" is close but incorrect — the key element is the WRONG BELIEF about one's REAL situation, not just general daydreaming.

t:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank. 
 Ashu is a dedicated guy, always ready to _________ for the betterment of his company.
o: snug as a bug in a rug
lose his marbles
rain on his parade
go the extra mile
e: D)'Go the extra mile'काप्रयोग होगा क्योंकि यह वाक्यांश वह संजीवनी उर्जा और समर्पण को दर्शाता है जो किसी कार्य में अधिक प्रयास करने के लिए जरूरी होता है। Ashuकी समर्पणभावना और उसकी कंपनी के लिए अधिक सेवा करने की इच्छा को व्यक्त करने के लिए 'go the extra mile' सबसे उपयुक्त वाक्यांश है।

t:
Choose the correct meaning of the bracketed idiom in the given sentence. 
I'm feeling a little _____ (under the weather) today, so I think I'll stay home from work.
o: Not well
Extremely well
A peaceful life
Generous and kind
e: The idiom "under the weather" means to feel slightly unwell or ill. It is often used to describe someone who is not feeling well enough to go to work or school, but who is not sick enough to see a doctor. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

(Hindi: अपनी अंतिम हार का सामना करना) Origin: The phrase comes from Napoleon Bonaparte's catastrophic and final defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, ending his military career permanently. Example: The president met his Waterloo at the election. The key distinction from other options: it is not just "any defeat" or "dying in battle" — it specifically means the FINAL, career-ending defeat.

t:
India and Bharat have both evoked the same emotions among patriots for decades, but these labels of pride have now been weaponised for narrow political ends. The Bharatiya Janata Party government at the Centre has decided to use Bharat instead of India in some official communication and documents, a practice that its representatives say will now expand. ‘India, that is Bharat,...’ is how the Constitution of India names the country, and the use of one or the other has been largely contextual all this while. The cultural echoes of Bharat have never been in doubt, and the current hype around it is more about a campaign to discard the use of India, as if both cannot exist in harmony. India, according to this telling, is a foreign imposition, and hence unsuitable for national dignity. Bharat, linked as it is to various ancient sources, goes beyond the geographical and cultural landscape that constitutes the modern republic of India. In that sense, both names are an outcome of India’s nation-building journey. Labouring to tease out the foreign from the native in the expanse of this nation that hosts a multitude of ethnic, linguistic, and genetic diversity and that has been formed as a result of millennia of migrations and cross-currents of human interactions serves no purpose other than creating new flashpoints in society.This farcical hubbub hoisted upon the country should have been allowed to dissipate and recede, but the knee-jerk reaction of the Opposition gave it the aura of a fundamental identity question before the nation. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh has been asking for privileging the use of Bharat over India for long, but the Opposition bloc’s decision to label itself INDIA as an acronym also might have influenced the BJP’s hurry in the naming exercise. Far from demonstrating a nation’s strength and pride, the government’s name game undermines the confidence and soft power of the nation. Bharat has been part of popular culture, political and cultural idioms, and literature across many Indian languages. Similarly, India is also used by millions within and outside the country who yearn for its progress. It is possible that contexts and constituencies of these proper nouns might vary, but that is the very reason to desist from attempting to impose the use of one and edge out the other. Whether it is India or Bharat, the essence of the meaning that it conveys remains the same. The needless juxtaposition of the two names should not affect the bonding of the inhabitants in the pursuit of a misplaced cultural combat. Let India and Bharat coexist as they have always been. 
 Based on the passage, what is suggested about India’s nation-building journey?
o: It has always prioritized the name 'India' over 'Bharat'.
It was only influenced by foreign entities, leading to the adoption of the name 'India'.
It encompasses a vast expanse of ethnic, linguistic, and genetic diversity formed from centuries of migrations and human interactions.
The Constitution of India only recognizes the country as 'Bharat'.
e: C) It encompasses a vast expanse of ethnic, linguistic, and genetic diversity formed from centuries of migrations and human interactions.

t: "His PhD degree seems to be (Penelope's web)."
o: An important task
A difficult task
A secret task
An endless task
e: The idiom "Penelope's web" comes from Greek mythology — Penelope, wife of Odysseus, wove and unwove a burial shroud each day to delay her suitors, meaning the task could never actually be completed. The idiom therefore refers to a task that is endless and can never be finished. "An endless task" means a task that seems to have no end or conclusion — for example, "Cleaning the beach of all the plastic waste is an endless task." This matches the idiom precisely. The distractors describe different qualities of a task: "an important task" refers to one of significant value (e.g., "Securing funding for the project is an important task"); "a difficult task" refers to one requiring a lot of effort or skill (e.g., "Completing the marathon was a difficult task"); "a secret task" refers to one kept hidden from others (e.g., "The spy was assigned a secret task"). None of these capture the specific "never-ending" sense central to the idiom.
